question.text: Find the integral of $\dfrac{2}{x} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ with respect to $x.$
question.explanation:
Applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

\[ \eqalign{ \displaystyle \int \left( \dfrac{2}{x} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right) \, \textrm{d}x &= 2\int\dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm{d}x - \int x^{-1/2} \, \textrm{d}x\\ &= 2 \ln |x| - \dfrac{x^{-1/2+1}}{\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}+1\right)} +C\\ &=2\ln |x| -2x^{1/2}+C. } \]

example.title: Integrating the Sum of a Reciprocal Function and a Power Function

question.explanation:
First, we apply the sum rule and get

\[ \displaystyle \int \left(x^{3/2}+\dfrac12x^{-1}\right) \, \textrm{d}x= \int x^{3/2} \, \textrm{d}x + \dfrac12 \int \dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm{d}x \]

Now, using the power rule in the first term, and taking out the coefficient in the second term, we get

\[ \eqalign{ \int x^{3/2} \, \textrm{d}x + \dfrac12 \int \dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{x^{3/2+1}}{\dfrac{3}{2}+1} +\dfrac12 \ln |x| +C\\ &=\dfrac{2}{5}x^{5/2}+\dfrac12\ln |x| +C. } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms

question.explanation:
First, we apply the sum and constant factor rules and take the coefficients out of the integral. We get

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int \left(\dfrac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x} \right) \textrm{d}x &= 10\int\dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm{d}x - \int x^{1/3} \, \textrm{d}x\\[3pt] &=10 \ln |x|- \dfrac{x^{1/3+1}}{\left(\dfrac{1}{3}+1\right)}+C\\[3pt] &=10\ln |x| - \dfrac{3}{4}x^{4/3}+C.\\ \end{align*}

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =10\ln{K}$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $10\ln|x|$ term, and we get

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int \left(\dfrac{10}{x}-\sqrt[3]{x} \right) \textrm{d}x &=10\ln |x| - \dfrac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{x^4}+10\ln K\\[3pt] &=10\left(\ln |x| +\ln K \right) - \dfrac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{x^4}\\[3pt] &=10\ln(K |x|) - \dfrac{3}{4}\sqrt[3]{x^4}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

\begin{align*} \int \left(1 - \dfrac{2}{x} \right)^2\textrm{d} x &= \int \left(1 - \dfrac{4}{x} + \dfrac{4}{x^2} \right)\textrm{d} x\\[3pt] &= \int \textrm{d} x - \int \dfrac{4}{x}\,\textrm{d} x + \int \dfrac{4}{x^2}\,\textrm{d} x\\[3pt] &= \int \textrm{d} x- 4 \int \dfrac{1}{x}\,\textrm{d} x + 4 \int \dfrac{1}{x^2}\,\textrm{d} x\\[3pt] &=x - 4\ln|x| + 4 \cdot \dfrac{x^{-2+1}}{-2+1} + C\\[3pt] &=x - 4\ln|x| - \dfrac{4}{x} + C.\\ \end{align*}

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C =-4\ln{K}$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-4\ln|x|$ term, and we get

\begin{align*} \int \left(1 - \dfrac{2}{x} \right)^2\textrm{d} x &=x - \dfrac{4}{x} - 4\ln|x| - 4\ln{K}\\[3pt] &=x - \dfrac{4}{x} - 4\left(\ln|x| + \ln{K}\right)\\[3pt] &=x - \dfrac{4}{x}- 4 \ln(K|x|). \end{align*}
